alt: Great blue heron spreading its wings as it lands in the water
remark: Males choose the nest site while the female builds it, often high up in mature trees above standing water to deter predators.

alt: Caspian tern in flight against a clear blue sky
remark: The red bill is what gives it away. Without it, easy to mistake for a gull at a distance.

alt: Mallard drake swimming in dark water
remark: The head only reads iridescent green in direct light, otherwise it's just dark. This is a handsome male.

alt: Mallard hen leading a line of ducklings across dark water
A Gadwall floats along in the water
remark: You might look at this and think, "ahh, the common female Mallard," and you would be WRONG. This is the Gadwall, which steals the food of the Mallard as soon as it returns from diving. Look for the fine vermiculation vs. larger brown patterning.

alt: Virginia rail foraging beside a path, with a worm in its bill
remark: Rails stay hidden, and I heard this one before I saw it. Also, they inspired the saying "thin as a rail!"

facts.value: Virginia rail foraging beside a path, with a worm in its bill

alt: Purple Martin perched at the entrance of a gourd nest box
remark: This is a male feeding some babies in a classic gourd birdhouse, which they're addicted to! They almost totally rely on humans for housing.

alt: Song sparrow singing from a bare branch against blue sky
remark: These are noisy birds that you've probably heard a hundred times, one of ~21 different species of sparrow found in the PNW.

alt: A Yellow Warbler sitting on a tree branch.
remark: The Brown-headed Cowbird will sometimes lay eggs in the Yellow Warbler's nest. Instead of raising the chicks, the Yellow Warbler will occasionally build a new nest on top and lay new eggs. One nest was found with six layers.

facts.value: They have one of the broadest breeding ranges of any warbler, from Alaska across nearly all of North America down into Mexico, with mangrove-dwelling subspecies in Central America and the Caribbean.

alt: Song sparrow perched on a cattail
remark: These little Pokémon build fake nests around their habitat to trick predators. This one is grabbing a bit cattail, probably to build one.

alt: Brown Creeper well camouflaged against a tree
remark: Because of their habitat and diet, their presence is an indicator of old growth forest health as those conditions are more prevalent in old growth forests.

facts.value: Flaps of bark on dead tress

alt: American crow perched in a conifer
remark: If you're walking around Capitol Hill and you're hear them going off above you, beware of swooping... they can recognize (or misrecognize) people and hold a grudge for years.

alt: A bald eagle with spread wings soaring
remark: The name comes from an old English word, balde, which actually means "white".

alt: Osprey soaring in a blue sky
remark: These bad boys will dive from 130ft at 40 - 50mph.
